claim: Official Uffizi admission is €25 same-day at the office and €29 pre-booked online; Uffizi+Vasari Corridor is €43/€47.
quote: Uffizi Gallery — Same-day purchase: €25; Pre-booked: €29; Uffizi + Vasari Corridor (same-day): €43; Uffizi + Vasari Corridor (pre-booked): €47

claim: There is no separate skip-the-line entrance at the Uffizi—all visitors enter through Door 1, but pre-booking cuts waits from 60-90 minutes to 15-25 minutes in busy periods.
quote: there is no separate 'skip the line' entrance at the Uffizi Gallery — every individual visitor... enters through Door 1. Pre-booked tickets cut total wait from 60-90 minutes to 15-25 minutes during busy periods.

claim: A new afternoon discount (entry after 16:00) and a Prima Mattina early-morning discount were introduced for the Uffizi in January 2026; book 1-2 months ahead in peak season.
quote: afternoon discount of €20 for entry after 4 PM introduced in January 2026... Prima Mattina ticket: €19 for the first two slots of the day — 8:15-8:30 and 8:30-8:45. Book 1-2 months ahead for 2026

claim: Accademia admission is €16 plus a €4 booking fee online (€20 total); a 15-minute timed arrival window is strictly enforced.
quote: Online advance purchases through the official Firenze Musei booking system cost €16 admission plus €4 booking fee, totaling €20 per person... a pre-assigned 15-minute arrival window strictly enforced by entry staff

claim: From 15 March 2026 a combined Accademia+Bargello ticket costs €26 (valid 48h) and a six-museum Accademia e Musei del Bargello pass costs €38 (valid 72h).
quote: Starting 15 March 2026, you can visit the Galleria dell'Accademia di Firenze and the Museo Nazionale del Bargello with a single ticket. The ticket costs €26.00 and is valid for 48 hours... €38.00 and is valid for 72 hours

claim: A David-only Accademia visit takes 45-60 minutes; a full visit including paintings and the musical-instrument collection takes 75-90 minutes; same-day tickets sell out by mid-morning in peak season.
quote: A complete Accademia Gallery visit... requires 75-90 minutes. Budget-conscious visitors focusing exclusively on David can complete their visit in 45-60 minutes... same-day on-site tickets face limited availability during peak season (April-October) when sell-outs occur by mid-morning

claim: In 2026 Palazzo Pitti opens 8:15-18:30 Tue-Sun (closed Mon), Bargello 8:15-18:50 Tue-Sun (closed Mon), and Museo dell'Opera del Duomo 8:30-19:00 daily except the first Tuesday of the month.
quote: Palazzo Pitti: 8:15 to 18:30, Tuesday to Sunday; closed Monday. Bargello: usually 8:15 to 18:50 from Tuesday to Sunday. Closed on Mondays. Museo dell'Opera del Duomo: 8:30 – 19:00, Monday to Sunday; closed first Tuesday of the month

claim: Bargello full-price admission is €12; its sculpture highlights include Donatello's bronze David and St George, and Michelangelo's Bacchus and Pitti Tondo.
quote: The full price ticket is €12... Don't miss Donatello's bronze iteration of the young David and his... St. George and the Dragon sculpture... Michelangelo's Pitti Tondo and the statue of Bacchus

claim: The Bargello holds the world's largest collection of Tuscan Renaissance sculpture and a focused visit takes about 45 minutes while a complete one takes up to 2-3 hours.
quote: the largest collection of sculpture of the Tuscan Renaissance in the world, including works by Donatello, Della Robbia, Verrocchio, Michelangelo... Allow about 45 minutes for a focused highlights visit, or about 2 hours for a more complete experience

claim: The Museo dell'Opera del Duomo is covered by the €30 Brunelleschi Pass (with Dome, Bell Tower, Baptistery, Santa Reparata crypt), valid 3 days; the museum has 28 rooms and a recommended ~90-minute visit and holds Michelangelo's Pietà and Ghiberti's original Gates of Paradise.
quote: Brunelleschi Pass at €30, covering all five monuments... The Museum consists of 28 rooms... with a recommended duration for the visit of approx. 90 minutes... original masterpieces including Michelangelo's Pietà... Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise

claim: Italian state museums (Uffizi, Accademia, Bargello, Pitti) are free on the first Sunday of each month but still require an advance timed booking for the Uffizi and Accademia.
quote: Italian state museums, including the Uffizi, Accademia, Bargello... are free to enter on the first Sunday of every month, though you still need to book a timed entry slot in advance for the Uffizi and Accademia

claim: The Duomo complex sells three passes in 2026: Brunelleschi Pass EUR 30 (Dome, Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata), Giotto Pass EUR 20 (no Dome), and Ghiberti Pass EUR 15 (Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata only).
quote: Brunelleschi Pass - €30 ... Dome, Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata; Giotto Pass - €20 ... Bell Tower, Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata; Ghiberti Pass - €15 ... Museum, Baptistery, Santa Reparata

claim: The dome climb requires a mandatory fixed timed slot (late arrival can forfeit it) and is 463 steps; Giotto's Bell Tower is a 414-step climb to 84 metres; the cathedral interior itself is free with no ticket required.
quote: The entry time on your ticket is fixed. Late arrival may mean losing your slot ... 463 steps from the Porta della Mandorla entrance to the lantern ... 414-step climb to the top of Giotto's Bell Tower (84 metres) ... the cathedral interior is free and always accessible outside service times

claim: Palazzo Vecchio museum admission is around EUR 13.50 for the museum alone or EUR 22 combined with the Arnolfo Tower; the museum opens Fri-Wed 9:00-19:00 and Thu 9:00-14:00, with the tower closing earlier.
quote: €13.50 for the museum alone or €22 combined with the Arnolfo Tower ... Museum opening hours are Friday to Wednesday, 9:00 AM - 7:00 PM; Thursday, 9:00 AM - 2:00 PM

claim: Palazzo Vecchio's Salone dei Cinquecento is a single hall 54 m long and 23 m wide, frescoed floor-to-ceiling by Giorgio Vasari and his workshop between 1563 and 1565 depicting Florentine military victories.
quote: a single hall 54 meters long and 23 meters wide, covered ceiling and walls with a vast fresco cycle of Florentine military victories painted by Giorgio Vasari and his workshop between 1563 and 1565

claim: Santa Croce adult admission is EUR 10 (2026), with a EUR 1 per-ticket online booking fee; children under 12, disabled visitors with companions, and Florence residents enter free.
quote: adult entrance fee is 10 Euros ... a booking fee of €1 for each ticket ... Children under 12 years old, disabled people and their companions, and residents of the City of Florence enter for free

claim: Santa Croce is the pantheon of Florence with nearly 300 tombs including those of Michelangelo Buonarroti, Galileo Galilei and Niccolo Machiavelli, and the standard ticket also covers the cloisters and museum.
quote: housing almost 300 tombs, including that of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli ... covers access to the basilica, tombs, cloisters, and the museum section

claim: The Medici Chapels standard ticket (around EUR 9 / USD 9 in 2025, plus a EUR 3 online booking fee) covers the Medici Crypts, Michelangelo's New Sacristy and the Chapel of the Princes, accessed via a separate entrance behind San Lorenzo.
quote: standard entry ticket is $9 full price for adults in 2025 ... includes entrance to the Medici Crypts, New Sacristy, and Prince's Chapel ... accessible by a separate entrance at the back of the church of San Lorenzo

claim: Michelangelo designed and built the New Sacristy from 1519 to house the tombs of Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, decorating them with his sculptures.
quote: The New Sacristy was designed and built by Michelangelo from 1519 to house the tombs of Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, which were decorated with his wonderful sculptures

claim: The current Ponte Vecchio is a medieval closed-spandrel segmental arch bridge dating to c.1339-1345, the only Florence bridge spared in WWII; in 1593 Grand Duke Ferdinando I evicted the butchers in favour of goldsmiths and silversmiths, and the Vasari Corridor (1565) runs above it.
quote: the only bridge in Florence spared from destruction during World War II ... Ferdinando I ... issued a decree in 1593 evicting the artisans ... in favour of goldsmiths and silversmiths ... In 1565 Cosimo I de' Medici had Giorgio Vasari build the Vasari Corridor

claim: Many of the Ponte Vecchio goldsmith shops are still run by families that have worked there for generations, keeping traditional craftsmanship alive; the Vasari Corridor reopened in 2024 for guided visits.
quote: many of them are still run by families who have been working there for generations ... the Vasari Corridor reopened in 2024 for guided visits

claim: San Miniato al Monte sits higher than Piazzale Michelangelo, is far less crowded, is a functioning Romanesque church dating to 1018, and is free to visit.
quote: while there are certainly plenty of fellow travelers here, it's not nearly as crowded by comparison ... dates back to the year 1018 ... The church and cemetery are free to visit.

claim: Piazzale Michelangelo is Florence's best-known sunset terrace with the postcard view of the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio, Ponte Vecchio and the Arno lined up, but it is the most crowded spot at golden hour.
quote: Piazzale Michelangelo is the best known place in Florence to enjoy a sunset over the city skyline ... the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio, Ponte Vecchio, and the Arno all lined up perfectly.

claim: Boboli Gardens 2026 single ticket is EUR 10 on the day of entry or EUR 13 in advance; a combined Boboli + Bardini ticket is EUR 15, available only at ticket offices on the day from 3 March 2026.
quote: €10 if purchased on the day of entry ... €13 if purchased prior to the date of entry ... Boboli Gardens + Bardini Gardens ... €15 ... Available only at the ticket offices on the day of admission From 3 March 2026.

claim: Bardini Garden offers a panoramic terrace over Florence with a baroque flight of steps and a wisteria pergola that blooms purple in April-May; open daily from 10am, closed first and last Monday of each month.
quote: From the panoramic terrace, in front of the restaurant, you can enjoy a spectacular view of the city ... wisteria tunnel occurs in mid April - beginning of May ... Daily from 10:00 AM (closed first and last Monday of each month)

claim: The Oltrarno is Florence's artisan left bank, full of workshops where craftspeople make leather goods, jewelry, ceramics and handcrafted shoes, and it turns bohemian after dark.
quote: Oltrarno's winding streets hide a treasure trove of artisan workshops where skilled craftspeople preserve centuries-old Florentine traditions ... leather goods, intricate jewelry, ceramics, and handcrafted shoes.

claim: Piazza Santo Spirito is the core of Oltrarno nightlife, lined with bars and restaurants with aperitivo from 7pm onwards where bars serve complimentary appetizers with a drink.
quote: From 7 PM onwards, bars serve complimentary appetizers with drink purchases. This creates a social atmosphere where you can mingle with locals while enjoying Tuscan wines and traditional snacks.

claim: Artisans have worked the Oltrarno since the Middle Ages, and San Niccolo is the other buzzing nightlife and aperitivo spot, with neighbouring San Frediano labelled the coolest quartiere for hip bars.
quote: Artisans have worked in this part of Florence since the Middle Ages ... San Niccolo ... the other buzzing nightlife spot, and the place to go for an aperitivo ... San Frediano ... labelled the coolest quartiere in town

claim: Piazza della Signoria is Florence's free open-air sculpture museum and civic heart, dominated by Palazzo Vecchio and the Loggia dei Lanzi housing Cellini's Perseus and Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine Women.
quote: open-air sculpture museum ... dominated by the imposing Palazzo Vecchio and the magnificent Loggia dei Lanzi which houses wonderful original statues such as Cellini's Perseus and Giambologna's Ratto delle Sabine ... it's free and open all the time.

claim: Mercato Centrale Florence's first-floor food hall is open every day from 9:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m.
quote: every day from 9.00 a.m to 11.00 p.m.

claim: Mercato Centrale's ground-floor working market (butchers, cheesemongers, fishmongers, fresh-pasta makers, lampredotto carts) operates in the 1874 cast-iron-and-glass hall and closes early afternoon and on Sundays, while the upstairs food hall has 24+ artisan counters.
quote: The ground floor is a working market with butchers, cheesemongers, fishmongers, fresh-pasta makers and lampredotto carts ... The ground floor market closes in the early afternoon and is closed on Sundays. The upstairs is a modern food hall (opened 2014) with 24+ artisan counters

claim: Mercato di Sant'Ambrogio, Florence's more local market, is open 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. every day except Sunday, with outdoor produce stalls and an indoor hall of butchers, delis, bars and trattorias.
quote: Hours: 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. every day except Sunday ... Sant'Ambrogio is the oldest market in Florence, operating both indoors and outdoors. It offers a more authentic, local Florentine market experience compared to the more tourist-heavy Mercato Centrale.

claim: More than 180 wine windows (buchette del vino) are documented in Florence; Babae was the first business to reopen its window in 2019, and Vivoli reopened its wine windows in 2020 to serve gelato during the pandemic.
quote: there are more than 180 wine windows in Florence ... Babae ... It was the first business to reopen its wine window in 2019 ... Vivoli ... reopened its wine windows in 2020 as a means of social distancing during the pandemic, but this time with gelatos.

claim: As of February 2025 there were 161 wine windows within Florence's old city walls plus 27 just outside, concentrated in the Santo Spirito neighborhood; active ones include Babae (Via Santo Spirito 21R), Osteria Belle Donne, and Caffe Duomo's functional wooden window.
quote: As of February 2025, there were 161 wine windows within Florence's old city walls and a further 27 just outside ... Most of the buchette del vino can be found in the Santo Spirito neighborhood and the city center.

claim: Vivoli, the oldest gelato shop in Florence (founded 1930, four-generation family-run), serves gelato only in cups not cones, and in 2025 opened a dedicated Affogato Bar in the leased space next door.
quote: Vivoli has nearly 100 years of gelato making history ... is said to be the oldest gelato shop in Florence, founded in 1930. They don't serve their gelato in cones, just cups. In 2025, Vivoli leased the space next to the gelateria and opened a new shop dedicated exclusively to affogato

claim: Gelateria dei Neri churns small batches for a smooth, intense texture and is cited for matcha, salted caramel and pistachio ricotta cremino; Perche No! (Via dei Tavolini 19R) has served natural-ingredient gelato since 1939 with vegan options.
quote: Gelateria dei Neri is known for its creamy and rich gelato because the flavors are carefully churned in small batches ... Perche No! ... is a historic gelato parlor serving sweet treats since 1939. They make their gelato with all natural ingredients, and they have soy and vegan options.

claim: Bambi Trippa e Lampredotto, the oldest tripe shop inside Mercato Centrale (since 1890), was named Florence's best street food of 2025 by Il Forchettiere and prepares lampredotto from the raw cut rather than reheating.
quote: Bambi Trippa e Lampredotto was named Florence's best street food of 2025 by Il Forchettiere and is the oldest tripe shop inside Florence's Mercato Centrale. They've been preparing lampredotto since 1890 - starting from the raw cut, not just reheating it.

claim: Lampredotto is the cow's fourth stomach, slow-cooked with tomato, onion, parsley and celery and served on a broth-dipped bun with spicy or green sauce for roughly 3-4 euros; Trippaio del Porcellino at Piazza della Signoria and Il Trippaio di Sant'Ambrogio are top stands.
quote: Lampredotto is the fourth and final stomach of a cow, generally slow-cooked with tomato, onion, parsley, and celery ... Prices for lampredotto in Florence generally range from 3 to 4 euros.

claim: Over 50 traditional artisan workshops survive in the ground floors of San Frediano and Santo Spirito in the Oltrarno; crafts include paper marbling, bookbinding, leatherwork, jewelry, mosaics and wood restoration, with workshops like Rilegatori di Libri A. Cozzi open to watch paper marbling.
quote: There are over 50 traditional artisan workshops in Florence tucked into the ground floors of San Frediano and Santo Spirito that are technically open to the public ... Rilegatori di Libri A. Cozzi is one of the few artisan workshops in Florence where you can watch pigments dance on seaweed gel

claim: Giulio Giannini e Figlio has produced hand-bound books, marbled paper and stationery since 1856 using traditional techniques, and Oltrarno has hosted leather workers since the 14th century.
quote: Giulio Giannini e Figlio has been producing hand-bound books, marbled paper, and stationery since 1856, continuing to use traditional techniques ... Oltrarno has been home to leather workers since the 14th century

claim: Scuola del Cuoio, founded 1950 by Franciscan friars of Santa Croce inside the monastery (Via San Giuseppe 5R), is a working leather studio where visitors watch artisans and can take half-day short courses making a leather book cover, typically open Monday-Saturday 10am-5pm.
quote: The leather school was founded in 1950 by the Franciscan friars of Santa Croce ... The half-day course participants are given a smock to wear while the Master Craftsman teaches how to cut, assemble and finish a handsome book cover

claim: The San Lorenzo outdoor leather market beside Basilica di San Lorenzo and Mercato Centrale sells bags, belts, wallets and jackets; haggling is acceptable, ideally starting at 60-70% of the asking price politely, with vendors responding well to humour but badly to aggressive bargaining.
quote: Haggling is generally acceptable, especially in the outdoor street market section of San Lorenzo ... The standard haggling approach is to start at around 60 to 70 percent of the asking price, be polite and friendly

claim: Fiesole is reached from Florence by ATAF/AT bus #7 from Piazza San Marco, arriving in Piazza Mino da Fiesole, with an archaeological area containing a Roman theater, baths and Etruscan walls.
quote: Take ATAF Bus #7 from Piazza San Marco in Florence... about 20–25 minutes to reach the main square in Fiesole. The bus leaves you in Piazza Mino da Fiesole... Inside the Archaeological area you'll find the remains of Roman baths and the Roman theater

claim: Fiesole's archaeological area (Roman theater, baths, Civic Archaeological Museum) opens 9am-7pm April-September and admission is around €5-6 for adults; the Monastery of San Francesco at the top offers panoramic views.
quote: From April to September: 9am-7pm... The archaeological area, including the Roman theater, baths, and Civic Archaeological Museum, typically costs around €5 or €6 for adults... Walk up to the Monastery of San Francesco, perched at the very top of Fiesole

claim: Greve in Chianti is reached from Florence by Autolinee Toscane bus departing near the SMN railway station, taking about one hour, or by car via the scenic SR222 'Chiantigiana' road through the wine area.
quote: It is also possible to reach Greve by Autolinee Toscane bus from Florence... takes one hour... The recommended route is Route 222, the very attractive 'Chiantigiana' highway passing through the Chianti wine area

claim: Buses from Florence to Greve in Chianti are run by Autolinee Toscane (formerly SITA), depart roughly hourly, tickets cost about €3-4 bought before boarding from the station or a tobacconist, and no seat reservation is needed.
quote: It's not called SITA anymore—it's Autolinee Toscane (AT)... operates a bus from... Fortezza to Greve Piazza Trieste hourly. Tickets cost $3–4... You buy it at the bus station or from a nearby tobacconist. Seat reservations on this bus are not allowed, and not necessary

claim: In Greve in Chianti you can taste Chianti wines via self-serve dispensing machines at Le Cantine di Greve, and the nearby Castello di Verrazzano winery offers tours and wine-paired lunches reachable by bus from Florence.
quote: Within Greve, there is the old wine cellar (Le Cantine di Greve)... you can taste via wine dispensing machines most Chianti wines... near Greve and with a bus stop nearby from Florence is the Verrazzano winery where you can have a wine tour and full lunch with wine pairings

claim: Settignano is reached by AT bus #10 from Santa Maria Novella station every twenty minutes (about 25 minutes), arriving at Piazza Niccolo Tommaseo; it was where Michelangelo spent part of his childhood and offers panoramic views of Florence at Piazza Desiderio.
quote: The #10 bus leaves Santa Maria Novella station every twenty minutes and takes you to Settignano, with the journey taking 25 minutes... the town where Michelangelo spent part of his childhood... follow the sign on via Simone Mosca to the panoramic view at Piazza Desiderio, where there is a stellar vista of Florence

claim: Settignano's draw includes hillside villas such as Villa Gamberaia, known for its immaculately designed Renaissance gardens (visitable for about €15), plus walking paths down to Ponte a Mensola.
quote: Villa Gamberaia is best known for its lovely, immaculately designed gardens, which can be visited for 15 euro... You can follow the stairs down toward Via dei Ceci and Via Vecchia di Settignano for a 15-minute hike to Ponte a Mensola

claim: Sesto Fiorentino is home to the Museo Richard Ginori della Manifattura di Doccia, the oldest still-active porcelain factory in Italy (founded 1737 by Marquis Carlo Ginori), with a collection of nearly 10,000 porcelain and earthenware objects.
quote: The Manufacture of Doccia has shaped the territory since 1737, when Marquis Carlo Ginori set up his manufacture... nearly 10,000 porcelain and earthenware objects, including sculptures, drawings, and archival documents

claim: The Ginori Museum of Doccia in Sesto Fiorentino closed in 2014 after the Richard Ginori bankruptcy, was bought by the Italian State, and its reopening after refurbishment was planned for 2025; the front garden has been open daily 8:30am-7:30pm since May 2022.
quote: The Museum was closed in 2014, following the bankruptcy of the Richard Ginori company; it was recently bought by the Italian State... reopening of the Ginori Museum is planned for 2025... From May 2022 it is possible to access the garden in front of the Museum... open every day from 8:30am to 7:30pm

claim: Sesto Fiorentino, on the northwest edge of Florence, is associated with ceramics and the nearby Renaissance Villa Medicea di Castello with its celebrated gardens.
quote: Sesto fiorentino, discovering the land of ceramics

claim: Vinci, Leonardo da Vinci's birthplace, lies about an hour's drive west of Florence (roughly 50 km, beyond the 30 km scope), reachable by train to Empoli then bus, and houses the Museo Leonardiano plus Leonardo's birth house at Anchiano 3 km away.
quote: Vinci is located about an hour west of Florence by car... the easiest way to get to Vinci

claim: A direct Florence-Sesto Fiorentino tram line is planned but not yet operational, expected to enter service around 2029 with construction starting in early 2027; until then Sesto is reached by AT bus and train.
quote: The tram line to Sesto Fiorentino is expected to become operational in 2029, with construction starting in early 2027

claim: The Firenze Card costs EUR 85 for a 72-hour pass covering more than 60 museums in the Firenzecard circuit.
quote: a 72 hour pass to access more than 60 museums in the Firenzecard circuit

claim: The Firenze Card is generally not worth it for a weekend; it makes sense only if visiting at least 7-8 major museums, otherwise pre-booked individual tickets cost less.
quote: You're in Florence for at least 3 days! ... no clear cut answer if you're making a decision based solely on the cost of the card

claim: The Firenze Card is EUR 85 for 72 hours; Duomo sites are excluded but a separate Duomo pass costs about EUR 30, and a new Uffizi+Accademia combo ticket (EUR 26 for 48 hours) launched March 2026 undercuts the card for those only visiting those two.
quote: a new combo ticket (EUR 26 for 48 hours) launched in March 2026 is dramatically cheaper than the Firenze Card ... you can buy a separate Duomo pass for EUR 30

claim: Florence's accommodation tax is tiered by hotel star rating: one-star EUR 4 up to five-star at EUR 10 per adult per night, charged per person per night and capped at ten nights with under-tens exempt.
quote: one-star hotels at EUR 4, four-star at EUR 7.50, and five-star hitting a ceiling of EUR 10 per adult per night ... The charge stops at ten nights ... Under-tens are free

claim: Short-term rentals in Florence are taxed at a flat rate per night and must display a national CIN registration code on the listing.
quote: Short-term rentals are taxed at EUR 5.50 per night and must display a national CIN registration code on their listing

claim: Reservations for the Accademia and Uffizi are highly recommended; reserve the Accademia at least two months and the Uffizi at least one month ahead, as lines form early and peak slots sell out.
quote: Reserve your entry to the Accademia at least two months in advance, if possible; to the Uffizi, at least one month in advance if you want your pick of times

claim: Climbing the Duomo's dome always requires advance reservations, which eliminated the formerly normal long queues.
quote: Climbing the dome of Florence Cathedral always requires advance reservations ... before they were required for climbing the Duomo's dome, long queues were the norm

claim: Shoulder season (March, April, October) is considered the best time to visit Florence, with late September-October offering ideal 60-72F weather, manageable crowds, and 20-30% lower hotel rates than summer.
quote: late September-October combines ideal weather (60-72F), manageable crowds, and 20-30% lower hotel rates than summer

claim: Florence's historic centre is closed to traffic except residents, taxis and buses, with Piazza del Duomo, Via Tornabuoni, Piazza della Signoria and Piazza Pitti fully pedestrian-only in the daytime.
quote: fully pedestrian-only areas, with only taxis (and ambulances and a few others) allowed to move around in the daytime

claim: The ZTL Centro Storico is split into camera-enforced sectors (A, B, O, F, G) operating Mon-Fri 07:30-20:00 and Sat 07:30-16:00 with no tourist permit; fines are EUR 83 per camera and Sundays are unrestricted.
quote: Enforcement runs Mon-Fri 07:30-20:00 and Sat 07:30-16:00 (Sep-Jun), and the standard fine is EUR 83 per camera crossed. On Sundays, the ZTL is NOT active
